webTitle: Trump administration sued over threat to deploy federal law enforcement at voting sites

fields.headline: Trump administration sued over threat to deploy federal law enforcement at voting sites
fields.trailText: Civil rights groups say plan will make people ‘afraid to vote’ and violates the Voting Rights Act
fields.bodyText: A coalition of civil rights groups filed a lawsuit against Trump administration officials on Friday, seeking to stop them from threatening to deploy federal law enforcement officers to polling stations in the US midterm elections. The suit, led by the NAACP, alleges that by threatening to deploy law enforcement to survey elections and initiating new voter roll oversight, the Trump administration has violated a section of the Voting Rights Act which prohibits voter intimidation. “The result is predictable: voters across the country – particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens and members of mixed-status families – are afraid to vote, help others vote and participate in civic life,” the plaintiffs wrote in the complaint. Plaintiffs cited other examples of voter intimidation, such as Donald Trump giving a primetime address to exaggerate claims of noncitizen voting, the administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operations in communities of color, and the president’s efforts to create a national voter eligibility list. Friday’s lawsuit is the latest attempt by groups to stop Trump from asserting more control over US elections as the country heads into what is expected to be a competitive midterm in November. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said “those who are here legally and not breaking other laws have nothing to fear” and denied that ICE was planning operations targeting polling locations. “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action,” the spokesperson added. DHS denied allegations of law enforcement engaging in racial profiling, calling the accusations “categorically FALSE” and insisting that targets of immigration enforcement were whether a person was in the US illegally, not by skin color, race or ethnicity. The FBI declined to comment for this story. ICE referred the Guardian to DHS. A White House official pointed to the administration’s past remarks denying any plan to deploy ICE agents to polls in November. Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, told reporters in February it was “not something I’ve ever heard the president consider”. Kiersten Pels, a justice department spokesperson, said in a statement: “The DOJ has never said it would send federal law enforcement to polling locations. Any suggestion otherwise is fearmongering.” Federal law states that no armed federal officers or members of the armed forces may be placed at a location where an election is being held. So far, the administration has not sent any armed officers or military members to polling locations. But recent mixed-messaging from top administration officials has raised concerns among election integrity advocates. In May, Trump did not rule out the possibility of sending the National Guard or ICE officers to polling locations. Kash Patel, the FBI director, told lawmakers this week that the FBI “will not shy away” from its efforts to ensure elections are safe and honest when asked whether he planned to send FBI agents the polls. “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t,” he added, noting that “we’re going to house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices”. Earlier this month, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, told reporters ICE would not be at polling locations to patrol but could be present if there was a threat or if they were serving a warrant to someone. “As a nation, we have no need for armed presence at polling locations – our elections are safe and transparent, which has been the hallmark of our democracy,” said Kristen Clarke, general counsel at the NAACP, in a statement after the lawsuit was filed. “Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period,” Clarke added. Friday’s lawsuit is at least the second of its kind. Last week a coalition of groups, led by the League of United Latin American Citizens, also sued the administration seeking to stop it from deploying ICE officers to polling locations.

webTitle: Trump’s authoritarian mindset can’t handle dissent from his appointees

fields.headline: Trump’s authoritarian mindset can’t handle dissent from his appointees
fields.trailText: Defiance from the supreme court and the Federal Reserve chair in one week ... how ever will the US president cope?
fields.bodyText: “It’s not personal, Sonny. It’s strictly business,” Michael Corleone tells his brother, Sonny, in The Godfather. But for Donald Trump, it’s always personal. And he leaves this week feeling betrayed. First, the US supreme court rejected his effort to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president wrote on his Truth Social platform. “They are merely a shell of their original selves.” Then the Federal Reserve defied Trump by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, marking its first rate hike in three years. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, described it as “a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision”. The president lashed out again but was careful to blame the board rather than Warsh. Trump told reporters he had spoken to the chair. “I said you might ⁠as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political.” It was an effort to rationalise a shock to the system for Trump, who instinctively assumes that anyone he appoints to high office will be eternally in his debt and automatically do his bidding. It is a view constantly reinforced by his cartoonishly loyal cabinet, from defence secretary Pete Hegseth to attorney general Todd Blanche, who was previously Trump’s personal lawyer. Blanche held a press conference in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday and staunchly defended Trump. He was rewarded two days later when he attended a campaign rally in Gastonia, North Carolina, and heard Trump say of him: “He’ll go down as the greatest attorney general in the history of our country.” But the supreme court is a different matter. Its conservative majority includes three justices appointed by Trump during his first term. It has certainly given him plenty of wins in emergency appeals during his second term, lifting lower court orders that had blocked his crackdown on immigration, ban on transgender people serving in the military and dismantling of the education department. Perhaps that is why the defeats rankle and, to him, appear inexplicable. The justices struck down his far-reaching tariffs on nearly every other country and his restrictions on birthright citizenship while blocking his attempt to immediately fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. Last week, the court refused to allow Missouri to use new elections maps redrawn at Trump’s urging to help Republicans gain an extra seat in the House of Representatives. Then came this week’s knockback of his administration’s planned restrictions on mail-in voting, which Trump has long condemned as fraudulent while continuing to vote by mail himself. Of the nine-member court, only justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented. For the authoritarian mindset, this does not compute. Trump has become accustomed to snuffing out the first sparks of dissent among Republicans in Congress before the flames of rebellion can spread. He has taken a scythe to government departments and entities such as the Kennedy Center, which he is now threatening to demolish. But not even he can control his own appointments when they serve in institutions protected by America’s system of checks and balances. The irony is that they might be saving Trump from his own worst impulses. The Fed’s intervention, for example, is aimed at curbing the rising prices that are hurting Trump politically. Warsh explained: “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.” It may only be a matter of time before Warsh’s honeymoon period ends and he feels the president’s wrath. But the Fed chair may also be aware that time is be on his side: every day brings Trump closer to the point at which Republicans begin looking beyond him to 2028. Last weekend, Mike Johnson, the House speaker, said only that Congress will “debate and discuss” Trump’s promise to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans retain control. On Thursday Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, forcefully criticised the president’s deportation agenda in a campaign ad. Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, says: “We’re starting to see institutions like the supreme court and the Republicans in the Senate more consistently resisting him. This is the beginning of the lame duck session for Trump. This is the entry point for where it’s going to be: a sour grapes moment in Trump’s political career.”

webTitle: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards

fields.headline: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards
fields.trailText: Local communities are fighting back against the influence of conservative groups like Moms for Liberty in education
fields.bodyText: Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted. “There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county. By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more. As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said. So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene. And last month, they won. Progressive candidates beat opponents backed by or aligned with Moms for Liberty in school board races across the state – in many cases reversing gains made by the group in 2022. Of the 30 candidates the group supported that year, 20 have declined to seek re-election, have been defeated or will face runoffs in November, according to the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Florida. In Sarasota, home to Moms for Liberty’s cofounder Bridget Ziegler, progressives flipped the school board, with liberal candidates Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry replacing more conservative members (school board races in Florida are technically nonpartisan). Glover got more votes than either of his conservative opponents, but his race will go to a runoff in November since no candidate won a majority. When reached for comment, Moms for Liberty referred the Guardian to a public statement disputing the notion that the recent Florida election represented a loss for the group: “Moms for Liberty-endorsed school board candidates won or advanced in 11 of 15 races across Florida.” But the group had issued fewer endorsements than in past elections and declined to endorse any candidate in several counties. That included Sarasota county, where board chair Ziegler, who has been plagued by scandal, was not running for re-election. Meanwhile, organizers for Glover’s campaign and others say the elections in Florida mark a turning point, a rejection of rightwing educational ideology in a deep-red part of a deep-red state. And, they say, the victories hold lessons for progressives campaigning on the national stage in the midterms and beyond. “We know that a better future is possible,” said Sebastian Martinez, president of the Sarasota Next Gen Democrats, a youth organizing group that helped campaign for the county’s progressive slate. “We’ll work every day to get there.” Students step up and organize Glover wasn’t the only Florida parent concerned about the influence of Moms for Liberty over his children’s education. The group had success in 2022 by appealing to voters angry about pandemic school closures, and by joining the larger rightwing campaign against “critical race theory”. But Moms for Liberty’s popularity has waned since then, said Liv Coleman, a professor of political science and international studies at the University of Tampa. By the time Stephanie Vanos ran for Orange county’s school board in 2024, the top question voters asked her was: “Are you the one who wants to ban books?” “It speaks to the outrage at state censorship in our schools and the complete disrespect for the first amendment,” said Vanos, who won her seat that year. But that outrage had yet to be fully harnessed. Martinez, now 22, has been active in school board organizing since he was 16. He started Next Gen Democrats last year as a way to expand young Sarasotans’ role in Democratic politics. “I really wanted to see young people not just get involved in organizing, but to become part of the party,” he said. For youth, one barrier to political participation is money, Martinez said – they can’t afford to volunteer their time when they could be working a paid job. So to help recruit and retain young canvassers, the group offered $20 an hour. “The Democratic party is supposed to be a party of working-class people supporting working-class people, and so it only makes sense to then pay people to work,” Martinez said. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats recruited about 20 high school students to phone bank, knock on doors and distribute yard signs around the county, said Kennedy Cole, the group’s political director. They also helped decorate a school bus that drove around Sarasota on Election Day, getting the word out about progressive candidates. Students “were sick of what we’ve seen from our school board, and we knew that Megan, Beth and Jimmy would help return normalcy to it”, said Cole, a 17-year-old high school senior. “Students really worked their butts off to get those results.” It wasn’t just students. Youth organizers met regularly with other community activists, including a group of retired women who sent 7,000 handwritten postcards to Sarasota voters. A parents’ group invited candidates to a local park to meet voters while their kids played. Equality Florida spent $250,000 on mailers in support of candidates around the state who were facing opponents aligned with Moms for Liberty. “In order to do something like this, it takes a web of people,” Cole said. “It’s a lot of different people operating in their own ways.” ‘Tired of the chaos’ Whether they were knocking on doors or meeting families at the playground, winning candidates spread a back-to-basics message that resonated with voters across political lines. Cole likes to tell the story of a close friend whose conservative parents voted for liberal school board candidates “because they were tired of the chaos” that Moms for Liberty had brought. Sarasota schools’ statewide ranking had slipped since conservative activists took control of the school board, said Mayberry, a former teacher who won a seat representing Sarasota’s fifth district. “The focus came off of academic performance,” Mayberry said. She and other successful candidates campaigned to restore that focus. They ran on issues like school funding, academic achievement and support for teachers and students, Coleman said. “They really just focused on things that affected people’s everyday lives.” That approach could be instructive for candidates around the country, in November and beyond. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.” That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools. “We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.” But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole. “If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

webTitle: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms

fields.headline: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms
fields.trailText: The extraordinary danger is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process
fields.bodyText: For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms. Trump’s March order forbade the US Postal Service from delivering mailed ballots to anyone the administration deemed ineligible. The Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, would have devised that list of supposedly ineligible, noncitizen voters. On its face, the move appeared plainly illegal. One expert told the Guardian’s Sam Levine, “This is a wholly unconstitutional EO,” because ultimately the federal government cannot set election rules; only states can. The plan was full of logistical problems, too. A whistleblower told Congress earlier this month that the Postal Service simply didn’t have the ability to implement the system safely, and that the whole plan was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to Richard Blumenthal, the senator who handled the whistleblower complaint. State election officials also complained they would be unable to implement Trump’s restrictions this close to an election, even if they were deemed lawful. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun mailing out ballots before the supreme court ruled, and chaos would have reigned there and across the country had the court blessed Trump’s plan. But it didn’t – and that sent Trump into a furor. In a lengthy post on Truth Social, in which he called mailed ballots “corrupt and out of control”, he singled out the conservative justices who had gone against him on that issue and this year’s ruling on tariffs. (Only the justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from the mailed ballot ruling; Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, both nominated by Trump, did not.) “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” the president fulminated. His position is clear: the federal courts, the states that administer elections, the USPS – all of them should bow to his whims, regardless of what the constitution says. Trump has already shattered legal norms by appointing his former personal lawyer to head the Department of Justice and then continuing to treat him as a personal attorney. Just this week, in a remarkable scene at the White House, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, served the role of White House press secretary, answering a wide range of questions from reporters on behalf of the president. A day later, a smiling Blanche attended a Trump rally for the GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, flashing an enthusiastic thumbs-up from the crowd. The extraordinary danger of this moment is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process. Trump’s claims about mail-in voting are false, as the Guardian’s George Chidi explained. The Brookings Institution has found: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” But Trump has been obsessed with the issue since 2020, when mailed ballots – which are typically counted last – evaporated his slim lead in some key states on election night. (Incidentally, Trump has voted by mail at least three times since then.) And more Democrats than Republicans vote by mail, so restricting mailed ballots also tilts the playing field towards the GOP. State election officials are now working to assure voters that they can safely vote by mail this year, as Levine reported this week. But one can safely assume Trump will not stop pushing democracy to the brink. Watch this race: Florida’s 27th congressional district Trump won this Miami district by 15 points in 2024, when he aggressively promised a campaign of “mass deportations”. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican representative, easily held the seat, vanquishing her Democratic opponent by 20 points. But Salazar is distancing herself from Trump this time around. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says to the camera in a remarkable ad released on Thursday. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” She is facing a significant challenge this year from Eliott Rodriguez, a Democrat and former news anchor. Fact check During Trump’s speech address at a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday, which the Charlotte Observer described in an op-ed as a “dark, divisive” speech, he painted the Tar Heel state as a crime-ridden hellhole. “So nobody used to think of North Carolina as a dangerous state, criminally dangerous,” Trump said. “It was like North Carolina, it was beautiful, it was apple pie, right? And now it’s one of the most violent and one of the worst in the whole nation.” (An interesting pitch to voters: your state is the worst.) But crime has fallen dramatically in North Carolina. Don’t take our word for it: only hours before Trump’s arrival in Gastonia, North Carolina, the White House blasted out a press release correctly noting: “In North Carolina, crime fell across all four major categories in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year, including a 12.4% drop in murders, an 18% drop in robberies and a 23% drop in motor vehicle thefts.” George Zornick is the Guardian’s US political enterprise editor

webTitle: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

fields.headline: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: The Labour leader said he would assess his success by how his policies affected his constituency. From the cost of living to immigration, we look at how Makerfield voters feel about their MP’s choices
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Remember the Makerfield test? When Andy Burnham was elected as an MP back in June, he reassured wary voters that the constituency was not a “stepping stone” (to be fair, it was a bit) but a “touchstone”. He meant that the policies his government devised would have to matter on the high streets of Ashton and Hindley Green. “A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness,” he said. As the Commons breaks for the jamboree of high ideas, low gossip and crap karaoke that is party conference season, it’s a good moment to ask how Burnham’s early decisions as prime minister – he’s been at it under two months, right enough – meet that test and what it tells us about his government. I spoke to someone who, since that byelection, has immersed himself in the opinions of Makerfield voters, and those living in constituencies like it, Luke Tryl, UK director of the research agency More in Common. But first the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington. Russia | Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. UK politics | Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company. Royal family | The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death. Nature | A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century. In depth: ‘The top thing for people in Makerfield was that life was a struggle’ “Who cares what Makerfield man or woman thinks? I’m a Holborn and St Pancras via Caerphilly gal myself,” you might be muttering into your overnight oats. But here’s why it matters: Makerfield, like dozens of similar post-industrial seats in the north of England, is the sort of seat Labour used to win so easily they could put up a ham sandwich as a candidate. Things have since changed. The area voted to leave by 65% in the Brexit referendum, and in the May council elections, Reform won all eight council wards in the constituency with about 50% of the vote. In his byelection dispatches from Makerfield, Luke Tryl found a pervasive sense of being left behind and forgotten – despite being “at the centre of the universe”, as one constituent put it, for one frantic month of campaigning. According to the voters Tryl spoke to, the Makerfield test should consist of three elements: Burnham showing that he “gets it”; a record of delivery; and a national plan to address the issues that Makerfield residents share with people across the country. So how has Burnham fared on some of the early challenges he’s faced? Cost of living measures “The top thing we heard in Makerfield was a sense that too much of life was a struggle,” Tryl tells me. And More in Common’s polling has found that, so far, Burnham’s early cost of living measures are very popular across the country: 86% of Britons had heard about the bus fare cap, seven in 10 thought it reflected well on the government; about 8 in 10 had heard about the VAT cut on household electricity bills (amounting to an average of about £45 a year per household), and 67% said that it landed well. Voters in Makerfield-like areas are realistic, says Tryl: “They say: ‘£45 is not going to change my life’, but they see it as a statement of intent”. People who are slightly more engaged with politics specifically mention the budget as a test point: earlier this week Burnham warned of “difficult choices” ahead. The cut-through of these measures to voters is striking: “Part of it is just the ubiquity of Andy Burnham,” says Tryl. Most recent More in Common polling shows people are more likely to have seen him on social media than any of the other party leaders. A fifth of Britons (22%) have seen “Cool Dad” Burnham on social media in the past week, compared to 20% for Reform leader Nigel Farage. I’m fascinated to see that for under-25s that rises to 35%, compared with 13% for Green leader Zack Polanski, who is often touted as catnip for younger voters. Immigration More in Common polling in June estimated that 62% of Makerfield residents consider immigration to be a top issue, making it one of the most concerned constituencies in the country about that issue. Here, Burnham gets a mixed review. The idea of taking in refugees through capped, controlled routes is popular in Makerfield, where voters worry over a lack of control. That’s why Tryl argues that one policy that really does pass the Makerfield test is the community sponsorship scheme, part of Shabana Mahmood’s controversial asylum reforms. But while Burnham has won back Labour-Green switchers over the summer, he’s not been so successful with Labour to Reform defectors – and Tryl believes that’s because he has yet to move the dial on migration. Take, for example, the shift in people’s perceptions: 52% of Britons now cite concern that local women and girls would be at risk of sexual violence as the top reason why they’d oppose asylum accommodation in their area (previously, they were more likely to refer to pressure on services). In socially conservative areas such as Makerfield, voters feel this “much more strongly”. “I think this is an achilles heel”, says Tryl. Prisoner release It’s not just constituencies such as Makerfield where voters think the criminal justice system isn’t tough enough: across the country, nearly two-thirds of Britons think prison sentences are too lenient. “The case of Andrew Harper outrages people across the board,” Tryl tells me, “but particularly in somewhere like Makerfield.” So Burnham played a bad hand well, by explaining the competing priorities to the public, and taking time to examine options before finding a partial solution. “Taking the public on that journey – especially in Makerfield where people are very distrustful of politicians – was important,” says Tryl. Climate Burnham, who is now facing intense pressure over whether to approve oil and gasfields in the North Sea, wrote in the Guardian yesterday that the UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050. While Labour-Reform switchers in places like Makerfield are often deeply worried about climate change, there’s also concern that net zero policies will unfairly punish ordinary people. For many, the issue of climate change falls below more pressing daily concerns like the cost of living crisis. In this context, More in Common’s polling suggests the main test for Britain’s energy policies will be whether they can lower household bills. Party donations Tryl’s fieldwork has found that the public aren’t deeply engrossed in the minutiae of donations limits, although they do want the system to be fair. So Burnham’s early failure to support a domestic cap on donations is unlikely to be a decisive factor when constituents in Makerfield next head to the ballot box. But for the recipient of those crypto-millions, the damage has been done: more than one in three voters now name Farage’s “sleaziness and corruption” as a barrier to them voting Reform. Rather than the party’s core voters, who seem unmoved by the continuing financial scandals, it is Labour-Reform switchers in seats such as Makerfield whose faith has been shaken. But Tryl cautions against over-stressing the issue. “At the next election, if the status quo on cost of living, core public services, andimmigration still feels pretty bad, I don’t think donations in themselves will be an issue” he says. We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? I’ll be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com What else we’ve been enjoying I loved our pics gallery of eastern Europe’s socialist hotels, which I hadn’t read about until now. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Cracker of a You be the judge this week: Ayaan lent her brother Ahmed some money thinking it was for something important … then he spent it on a holiday. But does it matter what he did with the cash? Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Zoe Williams’s interview with academic/author/policymaker Camilla Cavendish, on all the reasons we’ve stopped having babies, utterly fascinating. Poppy In case you missed it, make sure you read this viral essay from The Cut (£) on friendless husbands and the wives who try desperately to build social lives for them. Charlie The photos in our piece on the Tate’s Edward Enninful-curated show, c, about how the 90s art and fashion changed British culture, are beautiful and nostalgic. Poppy Sport Cricket | England extended their extraordinary hex over Sri Lanka to a 14th game, Tom Banton and Harry Brook leading them to a six-wicket victory with 47 balls to spare in the second T20 international. Football | Two first-half goals inspired Bournemouth, playing in their first European match, to a 2-1 win against Real Sociedad in the Europa League, while Crystal Palace had a comfortable 4-0 win over Lech Poznan. Athletics | Keely Hodgkinson has lifted the lid on how plans to chase the 800m world record this summer were ruined by a freak accident that her team has likened to whiplash. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now Music Beabadoobee: Pylon | ★★★★☆ The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. Film Resident Evil (in cinemas now) | ★★★★☆ Weapons director Zach Cregger delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaos. Read Jesse Hassenger’s full review. TV 70 Up (ITVX) | ★★★★☆ The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegiac, thoughtful outing ever. Read Lucy Mangan’s full review. Games Marvel’s Wolverine | ★★★☆☆ Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore. Read Keith Stuart’s full review. The front pages “UK must fully commit to hitting net zero by 2050, says Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Labour’s tax raid on holiday cottages”, and the FT writes “BoE warns of higher rates ahead to tackle rising inflation”. On Earl Spencer’s claims, the Times leads with “Charles was elated after Diana died, earl claims”, the Mail splashes “Queen offered to restore Diana’s HRH … after she died”, the Mirror says “War of words”, and the Sun asks “Why is he doing this to the King now?”. The i Paper runs with “Palace on the defensive after Earl’s new claims against King”, and the Express has “Charles was ‘emphatic we respect Diana’s memory’”. Lastly, Metro says “A royal crisis? What crisis?”. The Latest Taking on Trump? Canada and EU forge closer ties Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has welcomed the EU’s proposal for Canada to become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’, despite threats from Donald Trump over the plan. The US president said Washington could impose ‘very serious tariffs’ or halt trade if the EU went ahead with the plan. But in a defiant speech to the European parliament, Carney called for ‘deep cooperation’ and said polling showed the overwhelming majority of Canadians supported closer ties with Europe. Lucy Hough speaks to Europe correspondent Jon Henley. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad West Yorkshire’s moors include beautiful pinks and purples; boast rich biodiversity and a variety of flora and fauna, and play an important part in tackling the climate crisis. But, before now, much of the area’s rural beauty might have gone unnoticed by the wider public. But, on Saturday morning, the Bradford Pennine Gateway Trail will open, the first reserve of its kind in West Yorkshire. It will showcase the area’s astonishing landscape, and it is hoped that it inspires people to explore more in the region. Writer Chris Moss described a trip to the area as embodying a “ local, low-carbon, cheap-as-chips tourism before the jet age” kind of throwback vibe, adding that the new route could offer “a model for how we travel in the future” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

webTitle: US Institute of Peace files emergency motion to block carving of Trump’s name into facade of its headquarters – as it happened

fields.headline: US Institute of Peace files emergency motion to block carving of Trump’s name into facade of its headquarters – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This is where we end, for the day, our live coverage of the second Trump administration. Here are the latest developments: A canvasser for a Maine PAC who was paid to knock on doors in support of Republican senator Susan Collins faces criminal charges after being caught on a doorbell camera stealing a package from an absent homeowner’s porch. Donald Trump admitted that he had no idea what lead ammunition is after he signed an executive order permitting its use by hunters on federal lands, reversing a policy that was intended to protect bald eagles from ingesting lead and dying. Democrats pointed out that María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican who released a campaign ad telling Trump some of his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” voted to spend $70bn on immigration enforcement. A federal judge issued an order requiring the Trump administration to give notice before making any major changes to Kennedy Center. A canvasser for a Maine political action committee who was paid to knock on doors in support of Republican senator Susan Collins faces criminal charges after being caught on a doorbell camera stealing a package from an absent homeowner’s porch in Woolwich, Maine on Wednesday afternoon. Video of the man, dressed in a red T-shirt with the name of the PAC, Stronger Maine, on the front and the name of the candidate, Susan Collins, on the back went viral after it was posted on Facebook by the homeowner. Stronger Maine called the police and fired the canvasser immediately, a source who has worked with the group told the Bangor Daily News. The Collins campaign said that the man was not employed by them. According to Federal Election Commission records, more than half of Stronger Maine’s $2.6m in fundraising this year has come from from the Virginia-based conservative dark-money group Stronger America, which donated $1.4m. Andy O’Brien, the former managing editor of a Rockland, Maine newspaper, pointed out on social media that the canvasser did a poor job of covering his tracks, because, before he grabbed the package and ran to his car, he left a flyer for Collins hanging on the homeowner’s front door. The canvasser, who appeared to have the Latin phrase “Si vis pacem, para bellum” (“If you want peace, prepare for war”) tattooed on his right arm, was later identified by the police and faces charges. “Thank you Woolwich residents and Facebook detectives,” the local shariff’s office said in a statement on Thursday. “The package thief/political campaigner has been identified and charges will be forthcoming.” The US Postal Service has stopped work on developing a computer system that was central to Donald Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the supreme court rejected the planned to change to how mail ballots are delivered this week, postmaster general David Steiner told the Associated Press. “There’s an injunction so we’re not doing anything,” postmaster general David Steiner said in an interview. Steiner, a former chief executive of Waste Management, Inc, said he is pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a “liquidity crisis.” Trump’s efforts to largely eradicate mail voting would have turned the postal service into an arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year’s midterm elections. Steiner declined to take a position on Trump’s policy, presenting himself as the leader of an “independent agency of the executive branch” whose influence over the president’s order was limited to operational concerns. “I don’t get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept,” he said. Donald Trump signed a pair of executive orders to expand hunting and fishing on Thursday which, he told a gathering of outdoor industry leaders in the White House Rose Garden, mean “opening up millions of acres of federal land for our hunters and fishers.” The orders seek to expand fresh and saltwater fishing and direct the secretary of the interior and other federal agencies to find ways to expand hunting, including of species not subject to certain endangered protection laws, within 90 days. Those agencies will then have 180 days to propose rollbacks to federal restrictions against hunting and fishing on federal land and to find ways to expand using that land for recreation. “This builds on our actions in August that opened up another 92 million acres of federal land across 32 states,” Trump said in remarks he largely read, and even hinted he did not entirely understand. “We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them and they weren’t able to,” Trump read aloud from a text he suggested his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, had prepared for him. “And this order also protects the use of affordable, traditional le-” Trump read, and then stopped to comment on what were supposed to be his own remarks. “Well, this is pretty good. Is that- I never knew this was a problem, Doug. You’re going to have to educate me, but you put it in,” he said to Burgum, before continuing to read the text: “lead ammunition.” The president then paused and looked up again to comment: “Is ammunition, lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s uh pretty good. I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: you wanted it, you wanted it, and I’m here for you,” he told the industry leaders assembled before him, who burst into applause. “So, the order protects the use of affordable traditional lead ammunition,” Trump continued reading. “That sounds good to me,” he said. As Trump spoke, the website of the US Fish and Wildlife Service, an agency within the Department of the Interior, still officially encouraged hunters to go “lead-free”, urging hunters to take advantage of “Lead-free ammunition incentives available at 26 refuges across 19 states” for the 2026–2027 hunting season. “Protect wildlife by choosing lead-free ammunition this hunting season. Encourage other hunters to choose lead-free ammunition for all hunting, including big game,” the agency urged hunters, as of Thursday night. The agency’s website even answers the question Trump apparently failed to ask: “Why choose lead-free hunting ammunition?” with the following information – now apparently to be discarded at his order: Lead fragments on impact. Lead ammunition loses weight as small pieces strip from the front of the bullet or shot as it passes through an animal. These fragments are found farther from the wound channel than you may expect, and many are too small to see with the naked eye, making them difficult to remove. Fragments reach scavengers. Lead fragments may be left in the remains after harvesting an animal, even after field dressing. Remains from field-dressed animals provide a food source for scavenging wildlife, including bald and golden eagles. Lead-free ammunition leaves less behind. When ingested, a lead fragment no bigger than a grain of rice can sicken and even kill an animal the size of a bald eagle. Lead-free ammunition leaves little or no fragments behind that could be consumed by scavenging wildlife. While Donald Trump ponders demolishing the Kennedy Center unless his name is added to the memorial for the slain president, the United States Institute of Peace filed an emergency motion in federal court on Thursday asking a judge to block his administration “from carrying out plans to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.” The filing was made in a court battle that began in May 2025, when a federal judge ruled that Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency”, or US Doge service, illegally took over the the non-profit thinktank created and funded by the US Congress through “blunt force, backed up by law enforcement officers from three separate local and federal agencies”. Musk’s Doge staff fired most USIP employees in a late-night email in March 2025, and then forcefully entered the thinktank’s building after cancelling its contract for private security. In court, the USIP has maintained the organization is an independent creation of Congress and outside the president’s executive authority. The administration argues it is an executive branch organization, and pushed ahead, last December, with affixing Trump’s name to the exterior of the building, using bolted-on lettering. That change already offended the USIP board members who filed the suit, but carving Trump’s name into the stone, they argued on Thursday, “would cause irreparable harm”. In the new filing, lawyers for the USIP argue that the administration, including Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have not followed the court’s order to maintain the status quo at the institute: Rather, they continued to dismantle USIP and to actively undermine the organizational independence enshrined in USIP’s organic statute— including by affixing the President’s name to the building. Unsatisfied with the relative impermanence of external lettering, Appellants apparently now intend to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of USIP’s privately owned headquarters building while this litigation is pending. The building—which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation— is a work of expressive architecture designed to be “symbolic of USIP’s “independent “mission.” Latvia’s foreign minister, Baiba Braže, has declared two Russian nationals, Alexander Ovechkin and Umar Kremlev, personae non gratae, meaning that they are banned from entering the country. As the Guardian reported, Ovechkin, the NHL’s all-time leading goalscorer, appeared last week in a campaign ad for United Russia, Vladimir Putin’s parliamentary party, before returning to the US for another season as captain on the Washington Capitals. ProPublica revealed this week that Kremlev, a Putin-connected boxing official, paid for, and attended, Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebration on a private island in the Bahamas in May. In a letter to the NHL’s commissioner made public on Wednesday, a Republican congressman from South Carolina, Joe Wilson, expressed “serious concern” over Ovechkin lending his celebrity to support “the dictatorial political party of Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, who actively works to oppress the people of Russia by outlawing freedom of speech and fair elections.” Ovechkin, a longtime supporter of Putin, whose Instagram profile picture shows him with the Russian president, has attempted to cast his appearance in the party’s video as a patriotic act. In a statement to the media, the Capitals said that Ovechkin, while in Russia, “was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign”, without acknowledging that it was a partisan political ad not for the nation of Russia, but for the party supporting its dictatorial president who has waged a brutal war of aggression against Ukraine. On Thursday, Ovechkin responded to questions about his appearance in the campaign video with Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, the leading parliamentary candidate on the party’s list for upcoming elections, by saying, “I’m Russian and I support my country.” “I’m for peace and love,” he added. “They asked me to do that, and I said yes.” According to Meduza, an independent Russian news outlet based in Latvia, Putin’s political team first considered making Ovechkin a candidate for United Russia in the 2026 elections. The Russian business news outlet RBC reported that when Russia’s state-owned polling firm tested the hockey star’s potential candidacy, they found that he would have been more popular than three of the top five candidates who were eventually selected. “His results were decent,” a source close to Putin’s administration working on United Russia’s campaign told Meduza. “But not good enough for anyone to ask him specifically or force him to do it. And he didn’t want to do it. He understood it would take a lot of time… appearing in a video is easy”. As our colleague Chris Stein reports, congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a campaign ad recorded outside the White House in which she told Donald Trump that some of his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” and warned him that he is alienating Hispanics who supported him in 2024. Salazar is facing a tough re-election fight in a Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, where recent polling shows her tied with her Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, a former television news anchor. Democrats responded to the ad by casting doubt on Salazar’s apparent break with Trump over immigration enforcement. On social media, the Democratic party’s main account shared video of the congresswoman telling NBC News in April: “we have to fund ICE and DHS – ICE and Border Patrol.” “Don’t fall for her lies. María Elvira Salazar has stood with ICE every step of the way,” the Democrats said in a caption to the clip of her April remarks supporting ICE funding. Salazar was speaking at the time about the ultimately successful Republican effort to pass a $70bn bill to fund Trump’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants through the end of his term. When that funding bill narrowly passed the House in June, in a 214-212 vote, Salazar cast a crucial vote in favor of the measure to allocate $38bn to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), $26bn to Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and $5bn more to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) through September 2029. Aaron Fritschner, an aide to Democratic congressman Don Beyer, commented on Salazar’s criticism of Trump’s immigration crackdown: “Salazar is correct about this but she is saying it to Trump in a campaign ad for her reelection after silently empowering harm and suffering for two years and voters aren’t going to be fooled about what she is doing or why she’s doing it”. A federal judge issued an order requiring the Trump administration to give notice before making any major changes to Kennedy Center. The order, the judge said, was meant to avoid confusion after the Kennedy Center abruptly closed on Wednesday, raising fears Trump would follow through on threats to demolish the building if he couldn’t put his name on it. Canada’s Prime Minister welcomed an offer for closer ties with the EU, a proposal that drew Trump’s anger. The proposal — first made yesterday by the president of the European Commission — would see Canada granted a first-of-its-kind “associated member status,” an announcement that surprised European leaders and provoked President Trump to threaten new tariffs on the continent. Carney, giving remarks to European lawmakers gathered in France, seemed open to the plan in substance, and outlined places Canada and Europe could deepen ties, while those between Canada and its southern neighbor looked increasingly frayed. A Republican congresswoman publicly rebuked Trump on his immigration policy. María Elvira Salazar, a GOP congresswoman, made a stark break with the president in a new ad asking him to rein in the excesses of his mass deportation campaign, which she said had left Hispanic Trump voters feeling “betrayed.” Salazar is fighting for reelection in a heavily Hispanic district that was once safe Trump territory, but that has since started looking competitive. RFK Jr. headlined a gathering of anti-vaccine advocates in Washington, D.C. Children’s Health Defense, the organisation Kennedy led before becoming Health and Human Services secretary, welcomed its former leader back for an event in Washington, D.C. During his remarks, Kennedy touted how he was wielding his agency’s power to advance the movement’s goals from inside the federal government. Facing backlash, the White House withdrew Trump’s pick to lead ICE. The former nominee, Lance Schroyer, was a former Oklahoma state trooper and onetime security guard for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He’d faced pushback for not having any experience in the agency he had been put forth to run, during perhaps the most contentious period in its history. Trump spoke with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Wednesday as the two countries eye an end to long-simmering trade disputes, Politico reported on Thursday. A US official who spoke to the outlet described the call as “constructive.” The US and Mexico have been trying to hammer out disputes surrounding the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the North American trade pact Trump spearheaded in his first term but that he has since tried to revise. Not long after President Trump threatened to tear down the Kennedy Center unless his administration is allowed to slap his name on it, a federal judge on Thursday ordered him to hit the brakes. The order from U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper mandated that the Kennedy Center tip off the public at least 30 days before making any significant changes to the structure – such as demolishing it. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership calls safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies. But opponents fear that closing the center is a pretext for its demolition, or retaliation for Trump not being allowed to follow through on a plan for renovations that would see his name added to former President John F. Kennedy’s on the building’s facade. Trump has done a lot to stoke those anxieties recently. In addition to his recent remarks, the president was photographed on Air Force One reviewing what appeared to be plans for the center’s demolition. The White House on Thursday announced that it had withdrawn its nomination for Lance Schroyer, who President Trump had picked months earlier to serve as the new head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A former Oklahoma state trooper, Schroyer faced criticism for his apparent lack of formal experience working in ICE. His greatest connection to the agency appeared to be his previous stint on the security detail of Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary Trump chose to replace the ousted Kristi Noem. A White House statement announcing the withdrawal of Schroyer’s nomination gave no reason for the move. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s Health and Human Services Secretary and a longtime champion of the anti-vaccine movement, on Thursday addressed Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine advocacy organization he ran for years. On stage at the organization’s event in Washington D.C., Kennedy touted his efforts to bring his agency’s force to bear on vaccines and processed food. “For many years, you’ve asked questions from outside the government, as I did,” Kennedy said in a meandering hour-and-a-half-long speech. “And now I have the privilege and the responsibility of leading the department that can put the full weight of the federal government behind answering those questions.” He continued: “That’s what this department has done for the past 19 months, under my leadership, and under the leadership of President Trump.” Kennedy reassured the audience that he would continue to represent their interests, and that they “have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” He touched only once on the measles outbreak that recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, arguing that Americans should care about children “who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries” as much as those who die of infectious diseases. Jon Kyl, a longtime Republican congressman from Arizona, died on Thursday, his family said in a statement. Over three decades in Congress – first as a member of the House of Representatives, and later of the Senate – Kyl established himself as a quiet titan of Arizona politics. His family attributed his cause of death to complications from a neurological disease. Kyl announced in a statement late last year that he would be withdrawing from public life after being “diagnosed with a neurological disease manifesting as dementia.” “We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity, and wonder,” Kyl’s family said in the statement. “Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected. We are grateful for his full and meaningful public life.” Kyl first joined the House of Representatives in 1987, an office he held before winning election to the Senate in 1995. He held his Senate seat until his retirement 2013, briefly returning by appointment in 2018 after the death of fellow Arizona senator John McCain. Representative Thomas Massie opened with a joke about his colleague’s return to Congress: “Senator [Mitch] McConnell has inspired my latest bill. It’s a term limit bill called Three Strokes and You’re Out,” he said. “Some people try to say that I’m not effective enough up here. I’m so effective they had to take two and a half weeks off of the calendar to stop me,” Massie said. He said he’s calling the unexpected House recess “the Hegseth Holiday” because he’s unable to introduce articles of impeachment against the US defense secretary until after the midterms. Massie says he called a newly elected Trump to ask him for the agriculture secretary position. Referring to RFK Jr, Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record. Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats. A top official at the Kennedy Center said that he closed the institution temporarily due to “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration” of the aging building. Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director and chief operating officer, said in a federal court filing seen by the Associated Press that the building will be closed for at least seven days to “assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration”. The temporary closure, which occurred without notice yesterday, is separate from a vote on Tuesday by the Kennedy Center’s Trump-picked board to close the performing arts center indefinitely for repairs. It was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he said. The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by Democratic congresswoman, Joyce Beatty, who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building’s “unlawful closing’. Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Donald Trump’s name from being added to the facade of the building. Beatty told MSNOW she had a verbal confrontation with the president on Tuesday during a virtual board meeting. The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the center after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building. Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said yesterday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, “because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.” Congress has allocated $257m to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building. As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades mounts, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is headlining the Washington, D.C., conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly two decades. Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government. Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), brings unusual attention to the conference, said Mary Holland, current CEO of Children’s Health Defense (CHD). “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” she said at the event on Thursday. The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. “Never, never surrender,” said Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism. Recent polling suggests that one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year and four people in Pennsylvania recently. Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death. Paul repeated incorrect statements that only elderly people died from Covid, but he also suggested that deaths among those who were “thin and healthy” may have been attributed to genetic factors, proposing genetic testing to determine vulnerabilities. “There probably is in all likelihood some genotype that predisposes you to this,” Paul theorized. “If you could go in and figure out a genetic test -- those are the things we should be looking for.” Anti-vaccine activists became nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. He praised Rand Paul for bringing the anti-vaccine conversation back to the national stage. Kane urged attendees to comment on the proposed HHS changes to the way it recommends vaccines, which experts say could sow confusion and chaos. “As we’re turning the corner and looking at the midterm elections, and this is now top priority -- I mean, sometimes I gotta pinch myself,” Kane said. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner... Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.” A Senate panel on Thursday voted in favor of President Trump’s pick to head the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, advancing him to face a vote by the full chamber, Reuters reported. If his nomination clears the Senate, Brian Johnson – an executive for the banking giant Capital One – would become the head of an agency charged with protecting American consumers from abuses in the financial sector. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from South Florida, made a rare public break with President Trump in a new ad, pushing back against Trump’s hardline immigration policy. “Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said, speaking directly into the camera. Salazar’s ad, framed as a personal message to Trump, highlights the large percentage of people recently detained by ICE who had no criminal record – part of Trump’s aggressive mass deportation campaign that voters have increasingly soured on. “Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy,” Rep. Salazar told Trump, looking directly into the camera. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Salazar continued: “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” Salazar’s rebuke comes as Trump is making every effort to make the midterm elections a referendum on his second term in office, a prospect that has worried some Republicans concerned about the president’s waning popularity dragging down their odds. New polling shows that margins in Texas and Michigan’s key Senate races remain razor-thin, with Democrats just narrowly in the lead. The new poll from Emerson College and The Hill puts James Talarico, the Democratic challenger in Texas, up by just one percent against Republican nominee Ken Paxton. The prospect of flipping a Senate seat in deep-red Texas has long seemed a Democrat pipe dream. The last meaningfully competitive Senate race in the state was 6 years ago, when former Texas congressman Beto O’Rourke came within three percentage points of ousting Republican senator Ted Cruz. But it’s seemed closer to becoming a reality ever since Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general, unseated incumbent John Cornyn in a primary race with President Trump’s backing. In Michigan, the poll found that progressive firebrand Abdul El-Sayed is faring slightly better against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, with El-Sayed winning 48 percent of respondents’ support compared to Rogers’ 46 percent. Rogers, the poll found, wins out with non-college educated voters and older Michiganders, while El-Sayed is ahead with independents. The Texas poll found that Democrats haven’t won over as many voters in the state’s race for governor, with challenger Gina Hinojosa lagging sitting governor Greg Abbott by 3 percent. A group of Democratic senators is demanding information from the Trump administration about what’s being done with massive oil revenues funneled to the US from Venezuela, The Washington Post reported Thursday. The Post reported that three senators – Ron Wyden, Elizabeth Warren and Sheldon Whitehouse – directed a letter on the subject to Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State and a key architect of US policy toward Venezuela, and Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary. The senators said that the Trump administration has kept Americans in the dark about where the money is going and what measures – if any – are in place to prevent its misappropriation. American forces arrested Venezuela’s longtime dictator, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise night raid back in January. Since then, the US has struck a deal with a new, more pliant regime led by Maduro’s former vice president to route a share of the nation’s oil sales to the US. Even as the Trump administration seeks to force regime change in Cuba through withering economic isolation, allies of Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, are angling to get rich off the island’s collapse. Reporting for The Guardian, Lee Schlenker and Ed Augustin found that business interests connected with Trump and Rubio, the architect of current US designs on Cuba, are jostling to fill the void left by companies squeezed out of the island by the latest barrage of US sanctions. A few key takeaways: A pair of Trump-friendly Texas business magnates are fighting to take over a Canadian company’s stake of Cuba’s mineral wealth. Sources close to the matter say that Trump Organization leaders, operating under a company closely tied to the president’s family, have traveled to Cuba to explore hotel deals after a pair of Spanish hotel chains fled the island. And Franklin Graham, a close ally of Trump on the evangelical right and head of the evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse, recently won a $40m federal contract to oversee the distribution of humanitarian assistance on the island Trump is pushing toward collapse. One source with decades of background in Cuba policy put it succinctly: “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail.” The Trump administration has taken an especially severe stance toward Cuba since the start of Trump’s second term. Rubio, the child of Cuban immigrants, has led that campaign, seeking to bring about his long hoped-for goal of collapsing Cuba’s communist leadership and seeing a new US-friendly government in its place. The goal of regime change in Cuba has echoes of the Trump administration’s playbook in Venezuela, where Rubio helped orchestrate the toppling of a leftist dictator and the funneling of the country’s oil revenues to US coffers. Speaking to EU officials in Strasbourg on Thursday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seemed open to a proposal to grant his country a new “associate member” status within the bloc – even as details remained thin on what, exactly, that would entail. “We welcome this ambition,” Carney said of the proposal. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments.” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, first raised the possibility of making Canada an associate member in an address on Wednesday.
